newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Mixed reports on effect of strike on Colombian oil.
newsitem.headline: Mixed reports on effect of strike on Colombian oil.

text.p: Union leaders and officials of Colombia's state-run oil company Ecopetrol issued conflicting reports Tuesday about the effect of a nationwwide public sector strike on production.

Hernando Hernandez, head of the 7,000-strong USO oil workers' union, said the strike, which began at midnight Monday, was "total" and that production, refining and pupming operations had been slashed by more than half.
National radio reports partially supported the union's version of the impact of the strike, saying that pumping operations were normal but production had been curtailed.

Ecopetrol's vice-chairman of production, Ismael Enrique Arenas said the industrial action had had no immediate effect on production and said administrative workers were filling in for striking union members.
The nationwide strike involves an estimated 800,000 state and already disrupted air-traffic, public administration, education and health services and telecommunications.

"The stoppage by USO workers is total. In terms of production and refining we have more or less been able to cut operations by 60 percent. In terms of pumping operations along the main oil pipelines activity has been reduced by about 50 percent," Hernandez said.
Alejandro Martinez, head of the Colombian Association of Oil Companies, said he doubted the strike would have much effect on private companies operating in association with Ecopetrol.
British Petroleum Co Plc and Occidental Petroleum Corp were not immediately available for comment.
Ecopetrol, independently of its private sector associates, currently produces about 411,000 barrels per day (BPD) of crude.
Throughput at its two major refineries in the oil center of Barrancabermeja and the Caribbean coastal port of Cartagena is about 260,000 BPD.

Colombia's main oil pipeline, which runs from occidental Petroleum Corp's in the east to the Caribbean coast terminal of Covenas has a capacity of about 220,000 BPD. The Central pipeline, which serves the south of the country and the eastern plains region, pumps about 150,000 BPD.
The last strike by USO workers -- a 24-hour stoppage in October -- succeeded in paralyzing all pumping operations along the countries two main pipelines.
